tagline: Springs and steamboat towns along the St. Johns River corridor
intro: The River of Lakes Heritage Corridor links St. Johns River communities and springs, with Sanford and DeLand as major anchors. Multi-use trails often parallel the byway, and its spring stops include Blue, Gemini, Green and DeLeon springs. Florida Scenic Highways describes the corridor through its history, contemporary culture and natural features. The 156-mile corridor received state designation on March 12, 2009, followed by national designation in 2021.

Its communities had earlier depended on water transport: the DeLand area was originally accessible only by steamboat on the St. Johns. At Blue Spring, Louis Thursby operated a landing by 1868, and nine steamboats eventually served it on regular routes, carrying freight, mail and travelers. A narrow-gauge railway connected Orange City with the landing in 1881, bringing citrus to the wharf. That railway later became part of the Florida East Coast Railway in 1896; its paved-over bed is now Magnolia Avenue.

From Sanford, head toward DeBary and DeLand, with Blue Spring west of Orange City along the way. Continue through DeLand’s Woodland Boulevard historic district to DeLeon Springs, where the state park lies off County Road 3. Farther north, US 17 carries the corridor to the Volusia County line; SR 11 forms another leg, reached from SR 40.
notice: In winter, manatees gather at Blue Spring State Park.

moments.title: Blue Spring State Park
moments.text: Blue Spring’s 73-degree Fahrenheit water attracts manatees during winter. It is the largest spring on the St. Johns River, but it was also a transport stop. By 1868, Louis Thursby ran a steamboat landing here, and his wife Mary served as postmistress. In 1872, he built a two-story frame house on a shell midden at the mouth of the spring run. His son later added a third story. The park service restored the house to its 1915 appearance, and the maintained building contains historical displays. Shell middens line the riverbanks and the spring run.
moments.notice: The Thursby House stands on a shell midden at the mouth of the spring run.

moments.title: DeLand
moments.text: The Hatters’ name keeps a hat manufacturer in DeLand’s university story. Henry Addison DeLand, who made his money in baking soda, established DeLand Academy in 1883. DeLand himself never lived in the city throughout the year. An 1885 freeze destroyed the orange crop and left his Florida investments nearly worthless. He returned north and entrusted the academy to John B. Stetson, his friend and one of its founding trustees. In 1889, the institution became John B. Stetson University. Beyond campus, Woodland Boulevard’s 19th-century buildings form the Downtown DeLand Historic District.

moments.title: De Leon Springs
moments.text: The mill beside De Leon Springs is a reconstruction, not the original plantation building. William Williams established Spring Garden plantation in 1804, growing corn, cotton and sugar cane through the labor of enslaved Africans. The mill stopped operating in 1864; by the late 1800s, only its wheel remained. The building was reconstructed in the early 1900s and renovated in 1961. The spring’s name was also a tourism project: Spring Garden became Ponce de Leon Springs after the railway arrived in 1886. No known records link Ponce de Leon to the spring.
